function.name: generate_sea_foam
function.description: Simulates the creation of sea foam based on the agitation level of water, amount of organic material, and the presence of salt. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

agitation_level.description: The level of agitation in the water, represented by a scale from 1 (calm) to 10 (very agitated).

organic_material.description: The amount of organic material present in grams per liter. This is a float type value.

salt_presence.description: Indicates whether salt is present (true) or not (false) in the water.

temperature.description: The water temperature in degrees Celsius. If unspecified, defaults to average sea temperature. This is a float type value.

message.content:
The color of the sea varies widely depending on several natural factors:

| Factor | Typical Effect |
|--------|----------------|
| **Depth** | Shallow waters appear turquoise or greenish‑blue because they reflect more sunlight and scatter shorter wavelengths less than deeper areas which look darker blue or even black at great depths. |
| **Sunlight Angle & Intensity** | On bright sunny days with low sun angles (early morning/late afternoon), seas often take on vivid blues or greens due to scattering of light. Overcast skies produce muted, grayish tones. |
| **Water Clarity / Turbidity** | Clear oceanic water shows deep blue hues. When there’s sediment, plankton, algae, or other particulates, the water may turn brownish, yellowish, or greenish. |
| **Presence of Organic Material** | Algal blooms give the surface a green tint; high concentrations of phytoplankton can make the water appear almost emerald. |
| **Salt Concentration** | In very saline environments (e.g., hypersaline lakes or brine pools), the water might have a pale bluish-white appearance. |

So while “the sea” is commonly imagined as a brilliant azure, its actual hue ranges from clear turquoise near shorelines to dark indigo in open oceans, shifting dramatically when influenced by biological activity, weather conditions, or human impact.
